cards.text: Grab a seat, friend. This one's a song by Asaph, the chief of the Levites King David appointed to praise the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:4-5), and it's set for stringed instruments. Asaph opens by telling us where God is known.

cards.question: Asaph sings that God is known in ___, and His name is great in Israel.

cards.text: Then Asaph gets specific: God's tent is in Salem. After all my years in the back of a junk drawer, I get EXCITED when anybody has a real address.

cards.question: God's tent is in Salem. Asaph names His dwelling place too. Where is it?

cards.text: Right THERE, Asaph says, God did something to the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war. Me? My whole arsenal is a mustache.

cards.question: There in His city, God ___ the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war.

cards.text: Then the song hits a Selah, and when it picks back up, Asaph isn't talking ABOUT God anymore. Listen to who he's talking TO.

cards.question: When the song picks back up after the Selah, Asaph starts saying You. Who is he talking to?

cards.text: Asaph tells God, "You are resplendent with light." Then he brings up mountains filled with game, big and wild and full of life.

cards.question: True or false: Asaph says God is more majestic than mountains filled with game.

cards.text: Then Asaph looks out over the battlefield. The valiant lie plundered, and they sleep their last sleep.

cards.question: When Asaph says the valiant sleep their last sleep, what does he mean?
True or false: Asaph says the men of might could still lift a hand.

cards.text: Asaph says one thing from the God of Jacob left both horse AND rider lying stunned. Not just the rider. The HORSE too.

cards.question: What leaves both horse and rider lying stunned?

cards.text: So Asaph says it plain: "You alone are to be feared." Then he asks God a question that pretty much answers itself.

cards.question: Asaph asks God, "When You are angry, who can stand before You?" True or false: the answer he's pointing to is anyone brave enough.

cards.text: Then Asaph looks back. From heaven, God pronounced judgment, and the whole earth heard it.

cards.question: When God pronounced judgment from heaven, what did the earth do?

cards.text: The WHOLE earth went still, like a group chat right after somebody asks who's paying. And Asaph tells us why God rose up to judge.

cards.question: When God rose up to judge, who does Asaph say He rose up to save?

answers.text: All the lowly of the earth

cards.text: Then Asaph brings up the wrath of man, and friend, I KNOW wrath. You should see me when I leave a batch in too long.

cards.question: True or false: Asaph says even the wrath of man shall praise God.

cards.text: And the ones who make it through? Asaph tells God, "with the survivors of wrath You will clothe Yourself."
Now Asaph has a word for everyone listening, and it starts with something they make and then keep.

cards.question: Asaph tells his listeners to make and fulfill something to the LORD their God. What is it?
Asaph says all the neighboring lands should bring ___ to Him who is to be feared.

cards.text: Asaph ends with the rulers of the world. He says God breaks the spirits of princes.

cards.question: In Asaph's last line, God is feared by the ___ of the earth.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 9 quotes "You are resplendent with light.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The setup for card 8 gives the answer away. Saying Asaph 'isn't talking ABOUT God anymore. Listen to who he's talking TO' tells the baker he is now talking to God. That rules out 'The fallen warriors' and 'The kings of the earth' before the question is asked.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'Asaph says one thing from the God of Jacob left both horse AND rider lying stunned.' / 'Not just the rider.' / 'The HORSE too.' Only the opening card may run longer than two.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke does not share the core action of the verse. Psalm 76:10 is about man's wrath ending up praising God, but the joke is about Papa Dorin getting angry when he leaves a batch in too long. It also has him getting wrathful over a baking mistake, which goes against his always-positive, mistakes-are-learning character.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The setup 'Asaph ends with the rulers of the world' points straight to 'kings' for card 14. It also rules out the wrong answers 'farmers' and 'sailors', because neither are rulers.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The opening card says the 'Asaph' in the superscription is David's chief Levite musician (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). The superscription only says 'A Psalm of Asaph.' Some Asaph psalms (such as Psalms 74 and 79) describe events long after David, so the text may not settle whether this is the same man.
findings.question: When a psalm superscription names Asaph (or the sons of Korah, and so on), should Papa Dorin identify that person as the figure from Chronicles, or only say the psalm is attributed to Asaph and leave who he is open?
